title: Three patterns of misplaced trust in Rust std unsafe code
excerpt: Microsoft FORGE Lab identified three recurring ways unsafe code in Rust’s standard library can break safety guarantees.
body:
### A tiny slice helper that broke safety guarantees  

A few weeks ago a Rust developer observed a crash in a library that used only safe code. The failure traced back to a standard-library helper that accepts any `AsRef<[u8]>`, performs a manual bounds check inside an unsafe block, and returns the byte at the requested index without the usual safety net. The simplified implementation looks like this:

```rust
pub fn get<S: AsRef<[u8]>>(s: &S, idx: usize) -> Option<u8> {
    // SAFETY: the author promises that the manual check is correct
    unsafe {
        let slice = s.as_ref();
        if idx < slice.len() {
            Some(*slice.get_unchecked(idx))
        } else {
            None
        }
    }
}
```

The function assumes three things: the manual check never panics, the caller’s slice obeys the `AsRef<[u8]>` contract, and the underlying memory is valid. If any of those assumptions is violated, the unsafe block can produce an invalid reference, and safe Rust code that calls `get` can trigger undefined behavior. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab uncovered this pattern while scanning the Rust standard library with Hyenas, their AI-powered vulnerability scanner [Memory Safety Bugs in Rust Standard Library](https://forge-blog.github.io/posts/rust-std-memory-safety/).

The research identified three recurring ways that misplaced trust in unsafe code leads to memory-safety bugs. The sections below walk through each pattern, cite a concrete bug reported by the team, and explain why the issue matters even when the surrounding code is written in safe Rust.

## Trusting code not to panic  

Many safe APIs wrap unsafe pointer arithmetic behind a panic-free façade. The contract assumes that if the unsafe block encounters an error, it will abort by panicking before returning an invalid reference. In practice, a panic can be caught with `std::panic::catch_unwind` or suppressed by a `#[no_panic]` attribute. When a panic is intercepted, the unsafe block may continue execution with a dangling pointer.

FORGE Lab reported a bug in the standard library where an internal panic was unintentionally ignored. The unsafe code performed a manual bounds check, panicked on overflow, and then proceeded to return a reference that could point past the end of the allocation. Code that called the function through a safe wrapper could later read or write arbitrary memory, violating Rust’s guarantees.

The catch is that the safe API cannot protect callers if the underlying unsafe code assumes “no panic will ever escape.” Adding explicit checks or documenting that a panic may propagate prevents the silent slip.

## Trusting user-provided implementations  

Standard-library traits such as `Iterator`, `Read`, and `Write` let callers supply custom implementations. The library often calls methods on those implementations inside unsafe blocks, trusting that the implementation respects its contract. If the contract is broken, the unsafe code can allocate the wrong amount of memory or compute an incorrect pointer offset.

One issue the team uncovered involved `Vec::from_iter`. The implementation relied on the iterator’s `size_hint` to reserve capacity. An attacker supplied an iterator whose `size_hint` reported a much larger upper bound than the actual number of elements. The unsafe code used the hint to reserve space, then wrote past the end of the real data when the iterator yielded fewer items than promised. The result was a heap overflow that could be triggered from safe Rust code.

The source notes that “trusting user-provided implementations to be correct” is a common source of memory-safety bugs. The standard library does not re-validate contracts at runtime, so a malicious or buggy implementation can break safety even though the surrounding code is safe.

## Trusting the underlying system  

Unsafe code frequently calls into the operating system, for example, to map files, allocate memory, or create sockets. The standard library assumes that the OS returns a valid, properly aligned pointer or that error codes are checked before use. When that assumption is false, the unsafe wrapper can dereference a null or misaligned pointer.

FORGE Lab discovered a bug in `std::fs::File::from_raw_fd`. The wrapper called `libc::dup` to duplicate a file descriptor and then passed the returned integer to `File::from_raw_fd` without checking for `-1`, the error value that indicates failure. If `dup` failed, the code treated `-1` as a valid file descriptor and later dereferenced it inside an unsafe block, leading to undefined behavior.

The article describes this as “trusting the underlying system.” The fix required adding an explicit error check and returning a `Result` instead of silently constructing a `File`.

## Why the patterns matter despite Rust’s guarantees  

Rust’s ownership model and type system eliminate whole classes of memory-safety bugs, but they cannot protect code that deliberately steps outside those checks. The standard library’s safe APIs are only as sound as the unsafe blocks they encapsulate. When an unsafe block makes an unchecked assumption, about panics, trait contracts, or OS behavior, the guarantee evaporates, and even code that never uses `unsafe` can cause crashes or security violations.

The FORGE Lab’s findings are especially relevant because Rust is now a Tier-1 language at Microsoft, powers GitHub Copilot’s runtime, and is being adopted in projects such as Bun, Android, the Linux kernel, and Cloudflare. Billions of users interact with software built on these libraries daily, often without realizing it. A single soundness bug in `std` can affect many downstream projects.

## The takeaway  

Misplaced trust in unsafe code shows up as three concrete patterns:

1. Assuming a panic will never escape an unsafe block.  
2. Assuming user-supplied trait implementations obey their contracts.  
3. Assuming system calls always succeed and return valid pointers.  

When reviewing or writing unsafe code in the standard library, each assumption should be verified explicitly, add panic checks, validate size hints, and handle OS error codes. Those small safeguards keep the safe façade truly safe.
